name: Hair styling clay & pomade

lead: Hair clay and pomade shape and hold hair so a cut looks neat and styled all day. Pomade is traditionally greasy, waxy or water-based and gives a shiny, slick finish; clay is a related styling paste with a more matte, textured look. Both appear in grooming discussions as tools for the pompadour, quiff and textured crop.

Pomades are mostly petroleum jelly, mineral oil or lanolin, often with beeswax for stiffness; water-based versions use polymers and hardening agents. Wax-type products stay pliable and hold hair in place without drying out like alcohol-heavy gels. The evidence base is mostly product descriptions and history, with no clinical studies.

paras: People work a small amount through towel-dried or dry hair with the hands or a comb and shape the style, choosing a heavier or lighter hold for the look they want. Oil-based products need repeated washes to remove; water-based ones rinse out more easily.

Wikipedia reports that some styling-product ingredients can strip oils or build up on hair, contributing to dryness, and that petroleum-based pomades can take several washes to remove; claims about follicle clogging or hair loss rest on non-clinical sources. A 2023 measurement study of Beijing hair salons found that styling products including clay, wax and gel release volatile organic compounds.

angle.text: Clay and pomade hold and texture hair so a style keeps its shape, giving a matte or slick finish visible immediately. They are styling aids for a neater, more put-together haircut through the day.

lead: Hair clay and pomade help people look better by controlling how the hair sits: they add hold, texture and either shine or a matte finish so that a cut reads as a deliberate style rather than loose hair. A well-styled head of hair frames the face, adds apparent volume at the crown or fringe, and can disguise thinning areas, which is why styling products are a common early step in looksmaxxing routines.

Hair clay and pomade are styling products used to shape and hold hair. Pomade is a greasy, waxy or water-based product that gives a shiny, slick appearance, holds longer than most hair products and often takes repeated washes to remove [1]. Clay is a related product that works much like hair wax but contains real clay, giving a thicker, heavier, gritty-feeling texture and a matte, nearly shine-free finish [2]. Together they cover the two main looks men's styling is built on: the glossy, combed-back finish and the dry, textured one.

Traditional pomades were made from bear fat or lard in the 18th and 19th centuries, with petroleum jelly, beeswax and lard more common by the early 1900s [1]. Modern oil-based pomades typically contain lanolin, beeswax and petroleum jelly in heavy, medium or light holds, while water-based pomades use polymers and are easier to wash out [1]. The products are central to pompadour, quiff, ducktail and undercut styles, which returned to barber shops in the 2010s [1][3][4].

No clinical studies of hair clay or pomade for styling were found. The research that exists concerns side matters: emissions from salon hair products, measured in a 2023 Beijing study [5], and dermatology case literature on pomade acne and pomade crust from 1970 to 1981 [6][7][8].

paras: Oil-based pomades contain ingredients such as lanolin, beeswax and petroleum jelly and come in heavy, medium and light holds; lighter versions, historically called brilliantine, are shinier and give a wet look [1]. Hold and shine trade off: more wax means stronger hold and less shine, more oil means a wetter look and weaker hold [1]. Water-based gel pomades offer firm hold but are less malleable and often contain hardening agents, while some newer water-based pomades are designed to feel like oil-based ones but wash out easily [1].

Hair wax helps hold hair while staying pliable, and unlike gel, which mostly contains alcohol, is less likely to dry the hair out. It is sold under many names including pomade, putty, glue, whip, molding gum and styling paste, with texture and purpose varying by manufacturer [9]. Common waxes include beeswax, candelilla, carnauba, castor and japan wax, plus lanolin and ozokerite [9].

Wikipedia's article on styling products describes pomade as mostly petroleum jelly and mineral oil, often with wax, and lists gel, mousse, hairspray, volumizers and clays among the other categories. It notes that gel was popularised for spiky styles by punk culture in the 1980s [10]. Details of clay composition beyond its clay content are not given in these general references.

Wikipedia describes hair clay as a product that works much like hair wax but also detangles hair and leaves it soft. It usually has a matte or nearly shine-free finish, suited to a natural, dull look, and its defining ingredient is real clay, which gives it a gritty feel and a thicker, heavier texture than creams or pastes [2]. Most clays are described as salon-grade and cost more than consumer-level wax and gel, and the main drawback noted is that too much product or poor application can leave visible residue showing as streaks in the hair [2].

Ancient Egyptians used a fat-based substance on hair, and the Gauls are said to have invented a waxy, soap-like styling agent [1][9][10]. Landmarks listed in Wikipedia's styling product article include Alexander Rowland's popularisation of macassar oil in Europe in 1793, Edouard Pinaud's presentation of brilliantine in Paris in 1900 and Brylcreem in 1928 [10]. Morgan's Pomade was founded in the UK in 1873, and pomades were at their peak popularity from the 1920s to the 1950s, with brands including Murray's Superior Pomade (1925), Sweet Georgia Brown (1934) and Royal Crown (1936) [1].

Brylcreem was first made in 1928 by County Chemicals in Birmingham, England, as a water-and-mineral-oil emulsion held together with beeswax; its name combines brilliantine and cream. Its advertising used a jingle and an RAF airman image in 1939, and RAF members came to be known as 'Brylcreem boys'. When a drier, less oiled look grew popular, partly because of the Beatles, the jingle's wording was revised [11].

Early 20th-century undercuts were held in place with products as basic as paraffin wax by young working-class men, according to Wikipedia, and 1930s and 1940s versions had a swept or pomaded top [4]. Dixie Peach, a pomade popular with American teenage boys from the Second World War through the 1960s, is among the brands the pomade article names [1].

The pompadour was associated with rock and roll in the mid-1950s and 1960s, worn by figures such as Elvis Presley, Chuck Berry and James Dean, and Wikipedia says it was typically styled with heavy pomade or Brylcreem into a high, slicked-back quiff; a variant is the duck's ass or ducktail. It was revived in the 1980s through rockabilly and vintage subcultures and again as a trend from about 2011 [3][1]. The undercut, with short sides and a longer top, was revived in the early 2010s and by 2014 was fairly mainstream in the UK; versions in that decade were often slicked back or gelled up [4].

Pomade's comeback in the 2010s is linked to the disconnected undercut and to period films and television such as Peaky Blinders, with heavy-hold pomade suiting the longer top [1]. A movement toward natural pomades with shea butter, beeswax and plant oils has also been described, aimed at nourishing hair and scalp as well as providing hold [1].

Style choice is part of the standard advice on hair in appearance communities: matching the product to hair type and the cut (matte clay for textured, natural looks; pomade for slicked-back and classic styles; gel for firm spiky shapes) is discussed as a quick, reversible change. Volume-adding styles are also used to make thinning hair look fuller, though no study has measured this [1][10].

Hair volumizers, described by Wikipedia as shampoos, conditioners, sprays, pomades or lotions that add temporary body to thin or flat hair, belong to the same toolkit [10]. The pomade's pompadour, quiff and ducktail heritage connects modern use to mid-century grooming culture, and the 2010s revival alongside undercuts and fades brought it back into barber shops [1][3].

Wikipedia reports that most styling products do not damage hair when applied properly, but any styling product carries some risk of drying hair, and ingredients that strip natural oils or build up on hair may contribute to dryness or breakage [10]. Its pomade article says petroleum-based pomades can build up, clog follicles and possibly impede hair growth, but notes that these claims rely mainly on a hair-care retailer's blog rather than medical sources [1]. No clinical study of this was found. Traditional oil-based pomades often need repeated washes to remove, and water-based ones wash out more easily [1].

A 2023 study measured volatile organic compound emissions from 88 hair products sampled across 139 Beijing salons and reported emission factors of about 78.9 g/kg for hair clay, 70.3 g/kg for hair wax and 156.4 g/kg for hair styling gel [5].

A dermatology literature on pomade acne goes back decades: a 1970 Archives of Dermatology article named the condition, and German case reports in 1979 and 1981 described pomade crusts, including on the face [6][7][8]. The titles indicate that heavy oily products on the hairline and forehead have been linked to breakouts; the abstracts available are brief, and no controlled trial of modern products was found.

No studies found on hair clay or pomade for styling outcomes. Related work includes the 2023 salon emissions study of hair products, which is an environmental measurement rather than a clinical trial [5], and case literature on pomade acne and pomade crust from 1970 to 1981 [6][7][8].
